Offline editing, after six weeks of beta

Six weeks on 96 workspaces, and the question is whether it ships. Two decisions are open — what a full local store does, and how the rollout goes — and the board holds everything still outstanding, sorted by whether I think it should stop the ship; drag anything you read differently. Three changes to the announcement wait in the margin, and the announcement itself is yours to rewrite. Sign off and it goes out over your name.

clashes per 1,000 edits offline sessions median resync beta workspaces

What a reader sees

Nothing about the editor changes until the connection drops. Then the save state is replaced by a count of what is waiting, and a line under the document says where those changes are being kept. Click between the frames.

The number counts queued changes, not keystrokes: a paragraph typed straight through is one. Beta readers asked for a number twice in the first week, which is why it says "3 changes waiting" rather than "unsaved".

How it works

Every edit goes to a queue before it goes anywhere else. Online the queue drains as fast as the server answers and nothing about it is visible. Offline it fills, and the local store carries it through a closed tab. 

graph LR
  E[editor] --> Q[change queue]
  Q -->|online| S[server]
  Q -.->|offline| L[local store]
  L -->|reconnect| S

The store is capped at 40 MB a workspace. The largest workspace in the beta reached 31 MB, over six weeks and without reconnecting once, so nothing in the beta hit the cap. What happens at it is the first decision below.

The merge rule

Two people editing one document offline is the case the rest is built around. The rule that shipped in week 3 merges by field where the first two weeks merged by document, and the clash rate fell by two thirds the same week.

By document
Clashes when
both edited anything
Beta rate
6.4 per 1,000 edits
Asks the reader
every clash

Weeks 1 and 2. Two people working in different sections of one document collided, so the prompt arrived over edits that had nothing to do with each other.

By field
Clashes when
both edited one paragraph
Beta rate
2.3 per 1,000 edits
Asks the reader
63 of 494 clashes

What ships. Edits land beside each other unless they touch the same paragraph. Of the 494 clashes since it went in, 431 resolved with nobody seeing a prompt.

The 63 that did ask look like this, and it is the one screen in the feature a reader can get wrong:

Keep what I wrote offline Your paragraph replaces theirs. Theirs stays in history. Keep the version from the server Yours stays in history, and the prompt shows it so it can be pasted back.

@@ -18,6 +18,12 @@ export function merge(base: Doc, mine: Edit[], theirs: Edit[]): Doc {
   // both lists arrive ordered by the server's clock
-  if (mine.length && theirs.length) {
-    return ask(base, mine, theirs);
-  }
-  return apply(base, [...theirs, ...mine]);
+  let out = apply(base, theirs);
+  for (const edit of mine) {
+    const clash = theirs.find((t) => t.field === edit.field);
+    if (clash) {
+      ask(out, edit, clash);
+      continue;
+    }
+    out = apply(out, [edit]);
+  }
+  return out;

The function after the change, with the three lines the rule turns on marked: 

export function merge(base: Doc, mine: Edit[], theirs: Edit[]): Doc {
  let out = apply(base, theirs);
  for (const edit of mine) {
    const clash = theirs.find((t) => t.field === edit.field);
    if (clash) {
      ask(out, edit, clash);
      continue;
    }
    out = apply(out, [edit]);
  }
  return out;
}
The server's edits land first, always. The reader who was offline is the one being merged in, and that ordering is why every device replaying the same log ends up with the same document. Same field, not same document. Widening this comparison to the whole document is the old rule, and the old rate. The only path that reaches a person. Everything else resolves without a prompt.

How the iOS stall was traced

Fifty-four stalls across 2,140 sessions, all on iOS 17.3 and 17.4 and none on 17.2. In every one the queue had already handed the batch to the network layer and no response or error came back, so our own retry never fired. Backgrounding the app and returning releases it, and that is the workaround below. A reproducer that skips our code entirely — the vendor's client posting the same batch — stalls at the same rate, and that reproducer is what the filed report carries.

What a full store does

At 40 MB a workspace, something has to give. Nothing in the beta reached the cap, so this decides what happens to the first workspace that does. My recommendation is the first. Pick one to settle it; if you want a fourth behaviour, the box below takes it.

effort: donerisk: low Drop the oldest documents
At the cap
the least recently opened document leaves the device
Reader sees
a line naming what left, and how to keep it
Worst case
a document they meant to have offline isn't there

Editing never stops, and that is the whole point of the feature. A document that leaves is still on the server, so what is lost is having it here, not the work in it — and this is the only one of the three that does not punish a reader for not reading a banner. Pinning a document keeps it, and the line that says what left says so.

effort: 3 daysrisk: med Stop accepting offline edits
At the cap
the editor goes read-only until a reconnect
Reader sees
a banner saying editing is paused
Worst case
they are on a plane with the document they came to write

Nothing is ever dropped, and that is the cleanest sentence any of the three gives a release note. It also fails at exactly the moment offline editing is worth having, and a reader with no connection cannot act on the banner telling them so.

effort: a weekrisk: med Ask which documents to keep
At the cap
a picker, before anything leaves
Reader sees
a list of what is on the device, by size
Worst case
a dialog between them and their document

The most respectful of the three on paper. In practice it arrives without warning, mid-sentence, and asks someone who came to write a question about storage — and it still needs the eviction code underneath, for the reader who dismisses it.

How the rollout goes

The beta workspaces already have it. This is about everyone else, and the three shapes differ mostly in how fast the iOS stall reaches people who never agreed to a beta. I recommend the middle one.

Everyone on the day you sign off Ten percent for a week, then everyone An opt-in toggle until the iOS fix lands

The day itself, whichever shape wins:

  1. Turn it on for internal workspaces first thing, and leave it an hour. Every past regression here showed up inside ten minutes.
  2. Point the offline banner at the release note. The help centre page replaces it in the first patch.
  3. Send the announcement below.
  4. Watch queue depth and resync time for the first day; both are on the existing dashboard, and neither carries document content.
  5. Leave the kill switch in for two weeks. It stops new offline sessions and never discards a queue.

The announcement

Nothing in this announcement is settled yet. Three lines wait on your decision in the margin, and a line you would rather talk about than settle takes a comment like any other text. The first came out of the beta's support tickets, where "offline" was read as covering the whole product. The second states the storage limit, so it assumes the recommendation above.

Offline editing works throughout the product.

Offline editing covers documents. Comments, sharing, and search still need a connection, and say so when they don't have one.

A device holds 40 MB of a workspace. Past that the least recently opened documents leave the device, and a pinned document never does.

The third is a deletion with nothing in its place. I am proposing it because the sentence is a promise we cannot keep: uninstalling the app takes the local store with it, and anything still queued there goes too. It says otherwise in the one place a reader would quote back at support.

Nothing you write offline can ever be lost.

The 96 beta workspaces get this the day you sign off, with your name on it. Open the block with a double-click, or its ✎, and put it in your own words. What it says about storage and about the rollout follows the two recommendations above, so a decision that goes the other way sends me back to this draft before anything goes out. 

Subject: Offline editing is leaving beta

Thank you for six weeks of it. Offline editing reaches everyone over the
next two weeks, and nothing changes for your workspace.

Two things worth knowing. Documents you have opened recently are kept on
your device, up to 40 MB a workspace; past that the oldest ones leave,
and you can pin any document to keep it. And when two of you edit the
same paragraph offline, the app asks which version to keep rather than
picking one.

If you hit the spinner on reconnect that some of you reported on iPhone,
switching away from the app and back still clears it, and nothing you
wrote is waiting on that. The fault is in networking code we don't own
and we have reported it; the workaround ships either way.

Where sessions live

The monolith split leaves session state homeless: today it rides the app server's memory and dies with it. Three candidates, one recommendation — Redis with a signed-cookie fallback. Click an option — or Tab to its mark and press Enter — to decide; your pick reaches the agent directly.

Constraints

Support ran "log out all devices" 41 times last quarter, all but two of them inside an active takeover.
  • Logout must revoke immediately — support runs "log out all devices" during account-takeover response.
  • Session writes happen on every request (rolling expiry), so the store sees full request volume.
  • The team already operates Redis for rate limiting; nobody runs Dynamo-style infrastructure today.

Settled last week

How the session id travels was decided before this page and the client change is merged, so it reads as one line — open it if you want the alternatives.

effort: lowrisk: low Host-only cookie, SameSite=Lax Set by the auth origin, sent on top-level navigations; nothing to store client-side and nothing for a script to read. effort: lowrisk: med SameSite=Strict Tighter, but a session started by following a link from email arrives logged out — support saw this on the last trial. effort: highrisk: med Bearer header from local storage Works for the mobile client without a cookie jar; puts the id somewhere every script on the page can read.

Sessions become signed tokens; no store at all. Revocation requires a denylist, which quietly reintroduces the store — with the hard parts (replication, expiry) still attached, and the account-takeover response waiting on them.

With nothing stored there is nothing to list, so the support console loses its per-device Revoke and "log out all devices" waits on the token's own expiry.

Sessions in the Redis we already run, keyed by an opaque id; a short-lived signed cookie covers Redis outages for reads, so a blip doesn't log everyone out. Revocation is a delete — which is the shape support's "log out all devices" needs.

One table, no new moving parts. Every request writes a row (rolling expiry), so at our volume that's the primary's headroom spent on expiry bookkeeping — and a session outage becomes a database outage.

The two cookies

The recommendation rides two cookies with different jobs:

revocablenothing readable in itSession cookie An opaque id; the store says everything else. outlives a revocationsurvives a Redis blipFallback cookie A signed snapshot; outlives a blip, never a revocation.

One revision is waiting on you below: accept or reject it with the controls in the margin, and the next version carries whichever you chose.

The fallback cookie is read-only: it can keep a session alive through a Redis blip, but revocation, rolling expiry, and new logins all require the store. A revoked session survives at most the cookie's 5-minute lifetime.
The fallback cookie is read-only: it can keep a session alive through a Redis blip, but revocation, rolling expiry, and new logins all require the store. A revoked session survives at most the cookie's 90-second lifetime — short enough that support's "log out all devices" reads as immediate.

How we know the long tail is unattended

Thirty days of gateway logs. The eleven dormant integrations pin their user-agent to SDK versions from 2023 and 2024, none has fetched the migration guide, and neither brownout produced a ticket from any of them. We read them as cron jobs from the traffic shape: the same requests at the same minute past each hour, straight through the five-minute brownout.

Three ways to carry them past 30 June; I recommend the first, and the runbook and the email below assume it. Click an option to decide, or put what none of them covers in the box under the group.

The gateway can translate a /v1/records read onto v2 and reshape the response — renames, one date format, nothing stateful. That carries every records-only integration, and it is what makes Meridian's exemption cheap to honor: their September traffic rides the shim, not a v1 stack kept alive for one customer. /v1/search can't ride it — v2 search is cursor-paginated, and a gateway inventing page numbers over cursors would be a bug we own forever. Search leaves three integrations exposed: Ostrava, who are migrating anyway, and two from the long tail.

  1. Freeze exemptions on 30 May. The list is Meridian, and stays Meridian.

Export queue backlog, 12 June

A retry storm from one malformed workspace held the export queue for 94 minutes. No exports were lost; the oldest was delayed 81 minutes.

Detected
09:14, queue-depth alert
Resolved
10:48, poison job quarantined
Blast radius
exports only; imports and sync unaffected
exports delayed oldest delay exports lost

Timeline

Queue-depth alert fires Depth crosses 500; normal peak is 60. On-call confirms a single hot job The same export id retrying at the head of the queue, every 45 seconds. Adjacent deploy ruled out The 09:00 deploy touched imports only; the queue code last shipped in May. First fix doesn't hold Raising worker count clears depth briefly; the retry storm refills it because the head job still fails first. Poison job quarantined The workspace's export is parked in a dead-letter table; the queue drains at normal rate. Backlog cleared Depth back under 60; delayed exports delivered.

Root cause

The −1 came from a client upload predating the size check added in March. Two other workspaces carry one.

The export worker treats any failure as retryable. One workspace carried an attachment with a declared size of −1, which fails serialization every time; with retries capped by attempt count but not by queue position, the job returned to the head on each attempt and starved everything behind it. 

graph LR
  Q[queue head] --> W[worker]
  W -->|serialize fails| R[retry in 45s]
  R --> Q
  Q -.->|starved| B[1,204 jobs behind]
The fix is one classification: serialization errors are permanent, not retryable. Retryable failures also now re-enqueue at the tail, so no single job can hold the head again.

Follow-ups

  1. Classify worker failures as permanent vs. retryable; dead-letter permanents on first failure.
  2. Re-enqueue retries at the tail.
  3. Alert on a single job id exceeding five attempts, not only on queue depth.

Summary

The only paragraph most customers will read, and it goes out in your voice: double-click it (or its ✎) and rewrite it. 

On the morning of 12 June, exports were delayed for 94 minutes. Nothing
was lost: anything you exported in that window arrived late, but it
arrived. One stuck job held up the queue, and the fault was in how we
retry failures. We've changed how that works; the details are below.
We're sorry for the delay.

There is nothing you need to do. Every delayed export was delivered by 10:48 UTC; if something downstream of you noticed the gap, reply on your support thread and we'll pull the delivery log for your workspace.

What happened

Exports run through a queue. At 09:14 our monitoring flagged it backing up, and by 10:48 everything delayed had been delivered. The fault was in how we retry a failing export.

The failing job re-entered the queue at its head position on each retry attempt, serialized ahead of all subsequent export jobs for the duration of the incident window.

Each retry put the failing export back at the front of the line, and every export behind it waited — the longest for 81 minutes — on a job that was never going to finish.

The trigger was a workspace containing malformed attachment metadata that our systems did not expect.

I'm proposing the deletion because the sentence points at a customer's data, and the fault wasn't theirs: our validator accepted the attachment at upload, and our worker retried a job that could never succeed. The paragraph before it already says everything a reader needs.

Impact

Impact on 12 June, 09:14 to 10:48 UTC.
Exports delayed 1,204
Exports lost 0
Workspaces affected 412
Longest delay 81 minutes

How these read was settled in draft 2; the record is folded below.

Counts, not percentages "1,204 exports" is the incident as the affected workspaces met it. "0.9% of the week's exports" is also true, and reads as chosen to sound small. Percentages Honest about scale, and it holds only until a reply quotes the absolute number.

Timeline

Trimmed from the internal timeline to times and actions. The fix that didn't work stays in; leaving it out would be conspicuous.

Monitoring flagged the export queue backing up Cause found One export, retrying at the front of the queue. First fix didn't hold We added workers, which drained the queue briefly; the stuck job still failed first, and the backlog returned. Stuck job set aside The queue drained at its normal rate. Every delayed export delivered

What we've changed

  1. We no longer retry a job that cannot succeed; we set it aside and page a person.
  2. A retried job now rejoins the queue at the back, so no single export can hold up the rest again. Both changes shipped on 13 June.
  3. We are adding an alert on any one job failing repeatedly — on 12 June, nothing fired until the queue behind the stuck job was long enough to notice.

This writeup is the record of the incident, so when the alerting change ships we will note it here rather than in a new post.

Per-token rate limits

Moves rate limiting from per-IP to per-token, so one office NAT can't exhaust the budget for every client behind it. Four files, one new bucket table, no behavior change for untokened requests.

Shape of the change

gateway/
  limits.py  +38 -9
  middleware.py  +2 -1
  ratelimit.conf  +1 -1
  migrations/
    0042_token_buckets.sql  +5

The interesting part is gateway/limits.py:41: the bucket key changes from the remote address to the token id when one is present. Everything else is plumbing that key through.

The ceilings themselves

None of these numbers move. What moves is what they are counted against: a plan's ceiling used to be spent by every client behind one address, and is now spent per token.

Ceilings per plan, and what each is counted against after this change.
Plan A minute Burst Counted against
Free 60 120 the token
Team 600 1,200 the token
Enterprise 6,000 12,000 the token, per environment
Untokened 60 60 the remote address, as before

The core diff

diff --git a/gateway/limits.py b/gateway/limits.py
--- a/gateway/limits.py
+++ b/gateway/limits.py
@@ -38,9 +38,11 @@ class Limiter:
-    def bucket_key(self, request):
-        return request.remote_addr
+    def bucket_key(self, request):
+        if request.token:
+            return f"tok:{request.token.id}"
+        return f"ip:{request.remote_addr}"

     def allow(self, request):
         key = self.bucket_key(request)
         return self.buckets[key].take()
diff --git a/gateway/middleware.py b/gateway/middleware.py
--- a/gateway/middleware.py
+++ b/gateway/middleware.py
@@ -12,3 +12,4 @@ def attach(app):
     def wrap(request):
-        limiter.check(request.remote_addr)
+        limiter.check(request)
+        request.limit_key = limiter.bucket_key(request)
         return request
diff --git a/gateway/ratelimit.conf b/gateway/ratelimit.conf
--- a/gateway/ratelimit.conf
+++ b/gateway/ratelimit.conf
@@ -1,2 +1,2 @@
 burst_multiplier = 2
-bucket_ttl_minutes = 10
+bucket_ttl_minutes = 30
\ No newline at end of file
diff --git a/gateway/migrations/0042_token_buckets.sql b/gateway/migrations/0042_token_buckets.sql
--- /dev/null
+++ b/gateway/migrations/0042_token_buckets.sql
@@ -0,0 +1,5 @@
+create table token_buckets (
+  key text primary key,
+  tokens integer not null,
+  refilled_at timestamptz not null
+);

Why the prefixes matter

def bucket_key(self, request):
    if request.token:
        return f"tok:{request.token.id}"
    return f"ip:{request.remote_addr}"
Unprefixed, a token id that happens to look like an IP would share a bucket with that address. The prefixes make the two namespaces disjoint.
Existing buckets are keyed by bare address, so the migration renames them once at deploy; mixed keys never coexist.

Testing

  • Unit: bucket key for tokened, untokened, and both-present requests.
  • Integration: two tokens behind one address each get a full budget; two addresses on one token share one.

Both suites run under the rate-limit marker:

# the integration half needs the migration applied first
cd gateway && alembic upgrade head
pytest tests/ -m ratelimit --maxfail=1

Search relaunch, week 6

Indexing is done and dark-launched; relevance is the open question. The shadow comparison puts the new engine ahead on head queries and behind on long-tail, which is the expected trade at this stage.

p95 latency ndcg@10, head ndcg@10, tail index coverage shadow queries

Milestones

Reindex on the new schema Full corpus, verified against the old index by document count and spot checks. Shadow traffic comparison Every production query runs on both engines; judgments collected on the diffs. Long-tail recovery Blocked on the synonym table export from the old engine — owner found, ETA Tuesday. Cutover behind a flag 5% of traffic, then doubling daily if guardrails hold.

The long-tail gap

The old engine's synonym table carries fifteen years of manual curation; the new engine currently ships without it. On tail queries where a synonym was the match, we lose the document entirely, which is most of the −0.03.

Evidence: 61% of tail regressions disappear with the table patched in

A one-hour experiment loading the March export into the new engine's synonym slot recovered 214 of 349 regressed queries. The remainder split between stemming differences and genuine ranking changes.

Next week

  1. Import the synonym table export when it lands Tuesday.
  2. Re-run the shadow comparison on the tail set.
  3. Draft the cutover guardrails (error rate, zero-result rate, p95).

Standing policy

Tasks are scoped not to share files, branch from the same base commit, and merge one at a time after a test run against current main. Mechanical changes land on green; anything touching schema/, auth/, or a public contract holds for your word, however green the tests.
